approved: Aged Care (Living Longer Living Better) Bill 2013

The no voters succeeded in dismissing a motion that called on the Government to defer the package of the Aged Care bills until the Senate Standing Committee on Community Affairs has reported on its inquiry into the bills. Someone who votes aye for this amendment supports these measures. The majority voted no so the amendment was unsuccessful. **Background to Bill** In April 2012 the Labor Government introduced the Living Longer Living Better Package. This was in response to the Productivity Commission's Inquiry ['Caring for Older Australians'](http://www.pc.gov.au/projects/inquiry/aged-care). The Package consists of five Bills, of which the Aged Care (Living Longer Living Better) Bill is the main one. The Aged Care (Living Longer Living Better) Bill makes changes to aged care which include: 1. Changes to residential aged care 2. Removes the distinction between high and low level care for residential aged care 3. Establishes Home Care to replace existing community aged care packages 4. Means testing for residential and home care 5. New payments for care recipients and providers 6. Independent reviews of the legislation by 2017 More information on the Bill and the context surrounding it can be found [here](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/download/legislation/billsdgs/2429310/upload_binary/2429310.pdf;fileType=application%2Fpdf#search=%22r4980%22). Alternatively, information about the package can be found at the [Department of Health and Ageing](http://www.livinglongerlivingbetter.gov.au/) website. The text of the proposed amendment can be found [here](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;adv=yes;db=CHAMBER;id=chamber%2Fhansards%2F62418f05-bfae-4b21-b883-5566181dff26%2F0016;orderBy=_fragment_number,doc_date-rev;page=0;query=Dataset%3Ahansards,hansards80%20Date%3A26%2F6%2F2013;rec=0;resCount=Default).

Criticised the Aged Care (Living Longer Living Better) Bill, saying the government's claimed $3.7 billion investment is really a net $284.6 million once means-testing savings and redirected funding are stripped out, cited independent analysis finding a revenue black hole of more than $750 million for providers, and noted there had not been a single prosecution for rorting in five years despite the minister's implication of widespread abuse.

Backed the Aged Care (Living Longer Living Better) Bill, noting 20 per cent of his Hindmarsh electorate is aged 65 and over, welcomed the $3.7 billion Living Longer Living Better package, and said the workforce supplement could deliver pay rises of close to 18 per cent for personal care workers and nearly 30 per cent for registered nurses over four years.

Criticised the bill, saying the government cut $1.6 billion from the Aged Care Funding Instrument to fund a $1.2 billion workforce compact, cited industry estimates that only five to eight per cent of Productivity Commission recommendations were adopted, and said more than $3.5 billion in planned aged-care development projects have been shelved since the reforms were announced.

Opposed the bill, citing Standard & Poor's forecast that age-related spending will rise to 14.4 per cent of GDP by 2050, said the government's headline $3.7 billion aged-care investment was actually only $577 million in new money, and noted up to 60 per cent of aged-care facilities are operating in the red.

Warned that Australians aged 70 and over will rise from nine per cent of the population to 20 per cent, nearly six million people, by 2051, said the ratio of working-age Australians to those over 67 will fall from six to one in 2007 to 3.2 to one by 2047, and accused the government of racking up $172 billion in deficits over five years while its own surplus forecast shifted from $7.5 billion to $12 billion in a single week.

Opposed the Living Longer Living Better aged care bills, citing a $1.6 billion cut from the aged-care funding instrument at a time when costs are rising three to four per cent while subsidy rates increased only 1.45 per cent, and highlighted that the Euroa aged-care facility had to rely on a $250,000 donation from a volunteer-run op shop to refurbish its building without any government funding.

Criticised the Living Longer Living Better aged care package of five bills for adding red tape to rural providers without adopting most Productivity Commission recommendations, citing a $1.6 billion cut from the Aged Care Funding Instrument, a $1.2 billion workforce supplement tied to conditions he linked to union influence, and a rule cutting accommodation supplements by 25 per cent for facilities with fewer than 40 per cent financially disadvantaged residents.

Criticised the aged care bills as a piecemeal response adopting only a handful of Productivity Commission recommendations, noting the government cut $1.6 billion from the aged-care funding instrument to fund a $1.2 billion workforce compact while only 40 per cent of providers operate profitably, and outlined a coalition plan to spend $335 million over four years converting up to 3,000 bed licences into operational aged-care beds.

Criticised the Living Longer Living Better package for including only $577 million in genuinely new spending despite a headline figure of $3.7 billion over four years, and said the $1.6 billion cut to the aged-care funding instrument, used to fund a $1.2 billion workforce compact, would leave 89 per cent of providers facing irrecoverable revenue losses.

Argued the aged care package fails rural and remote electorates such as Durack, citing reports that up to 60 per cent of facilities operate at a loss and that aged care nurses spend a third of their time on paperwork, and warning that Australians aged 70 and over will nearly double as a share of the population by 2051.

Argued the Living Longer Living Better aged care package leaves key details to regulation and cut $1.6 billion from the Aged Care Funding Instrument with little notice, citing analysis finding funding reductions of between eight and 15 per cent weighted most heavily on high care and dementia facilities.

Argued the aged care package increases regulation while cutting $1.6 billion from the Aged Care Funding Instrument, citing an industry estimate of a $750 million revenue black hole and a survey finding 89 per cent of facilities will face unrecoverable revenue losses under the changes.

Accused the government of cutting $1.6 billion from aged care funding while introducing a $1.2 billion Workforce Compact that requires larger providers to enter union agreements to access funding, and said 3,500 aged care bed licences remain unused in Western Australia due to poor viability.

Raised concerns about the Aged Care (Living Longer Living Better) Bill, saying only 40 per cent of aged-care providers nationally are operating in the black after a $1.6 billion cut to the Aged Care Funding Instrument, and described his home town of Warialda using a $3 million low-interest federal loan to build a dementia-specific wing at its Naroo aged-care facility.

Backed the Aged Care (Living Longer Living Better) Bill and its four related bills, noting Australians aged 65 and over will rise from 13 to 23 per cent of the population by 2050, and said home care places will increase from around 60,000 to almost 100,000 over five years, with income-tested care fees capped at $60,000 over a person's lifetime.

Opposed rushing the Aged Care (Living Longer Living Better) Bill through before a Senate inquiry reports, saying aged-care providers across his Wannon electorate, many small not-for-profits built through community fundraising, had real concerns about the bill and felt inadequately consulted.

Rejected the aged-care bills, arguing the government's claimed $3.7 billion aged-care investment is really closer to $577 million in new funding, said up to 89 per cent of facilities face unrecoverable revenue losses under the changes, and accused the government of cutting $1.6 billion from the Aged Care Funding Instrument to finance a $1.2 billion union-linked workforce compact.

Contested the aged-care bills, citing the shadow minister's analysis that the government's claimed $3.7 billion investment is really a net $284.6 million once means-testing savings and $1.6 billion redirected from the Aged Care Funding Instrument are accounted for, and noted Australians over 65 will rise from 13.4 to 25.3 per cent of the population over the next 40 years.

Criticised the aged-care bills, noting the population aged 70 and over will rise from 9 per cent now to 20 per cent by 2050, said only 40 per cent of aged-care providers are currently profitable, and cited Baptistcare's warning that it would need to find an extra $3 for every $1 received under the government's workforce supplement.

Argued that the bills transferred funding from aged-care services into a workforce supplement while imposing financial risks on providers, including through a 28-day delay before residents choose payment arrangements. Criticised alleged union recruitment incentives and claims of sector rorting, and called for cooperative, properly funded reform.

Supported aged-care reform but raised the needs of older people who are homeless or at risk of homelessness, including outreach, intensive support and suitable environments. Praised Wintringham's specialised service and urged resolution of funding concerns before the package passed so its viability could continue.

Argued that the aged-care bills stated broad intentions while leaving important operational details unresolved, creating uncertainty for providers about pricing regulation, resident contributions, finance and workforce costs. Supported an amendment delaying consideration until the Senate inquiry reported, and called for evidence-based reform with more stable funding arrangements.

Asked why the aged-care bills were being rushed through when most provisions would not commence until 1 July 2014, and argued that they left provider viability, regulation and infrastructure problems unresolved. Reported continuing concerns at Star of the Sea on Thursday Island and advocated support for aged care in Mossman and culturally appropriate Indigenous services.

Announced that the government supported the five aged-care bills, describing them as a $3.7 billion package developed through consultation to provide greater choice, control, sustainable financing and oversight. Said the government would not support the opposition amendment and noted that a homelessness supplement remained to be developed.
